title: ISAs, Operating Systems (Betriebssysteme), and Virtual Memory (virtueller Speicher)
summary: This unit compares x86, RISC-V, and ARM in terms of registers (Register), calling conventions (Aufrufkonventionen), addressing modes (Adressierungsarten), and instruction formats (Befehlsformen). It then covers multiuser systems (Mehrbenutzersysteme), interrupts (Interrupts), and virtual-address translation using page tables (Seitentabellen), the TLB, and paging (Paging).
keyFacts: x86 is a CISC ISA with many complex instructions, variable instruction lengths, and support for legacy execution modes.
IA-32 refers to the 32-bit variant; x86_64, or Intel 64, is a later 64-bit extension that originally came from AMD.
The same x86 registers can be accessed as RAX (64 bits), EAX (32 bits), AX (16 bits), or AH/AL (8 bits each).
In the x86_64 calling convention presented, the first six parameters are passed in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, and r9; additional parameters are passed on the stack. The return value is in rax.
In IA-32, call places the return address on the stack; in RISC-V, jal typically stores the return address in ra.
With base-relative addressing, the effective address is the register contents plus the offset; with scaled indexing, it is the base plus the index multiplied by the operand size.
In the two-address form, the destination is also a source. In the three-address register-register form, the two sources and the destination are separate.
ARMv8 (AArch64) is ARM's first 64-bit ISA. The similarities with RISC-V described here include RISC, 4-byte instructions, and Load/Store.
Time sharing saves the state of an interrupted program, lets the scheduler select the next one, and loads its state.
Interrupts are asynchronous and triggered by external events; exceptions are synchronous and associated with an executed instruction.
The MMU translates virtual addresses into physical addresses during memory accesses; virtual pages can be mapped to noncontiguous physical frames.
With 4-KiB pages, the offset is 12 bits and remains unchanged during translation.
An Sv32 page-table entry contains, among other fields, V, R/W/X, U, G, A, and D. Invalid entries or unauthorized accesses cause an exception.
The X/W/R bit patterns 001, 011, 100, 101, and 111 represent read, read/write, execute, read/execute, and read/write/execute, respectively; 010 and 110 are reserved.
Multilevel page tables avoid having to reserve entries in a large single-level table for unused areas of the virtual address space.
A TLB caches recently used address translations; without a TLB, Sv39 requires three page-table accesses before the actual data access.
With lazy allocation, a virtual page receives a physical frame only after an access triggers an exception.
With paging, a selected page is marked as absent and swapped out; a later access triggers it to be loaded back. Pinned pages are not swapped out.

review.notes: 45 Fragen geprüft. Präzisiert: die Sv39-Frage zum TLB-Miss, die Bedeutung von U und X/W/R sowie die Byte-Reihenfolge bei Little Endian. Alle Rechenprüfungen und Antwortmengen stimmen; jedes Level hat mindestens 8 Fragen.

questions.prompt: Which description applies to x86?

options.text: A CISC ISA with complex instructions and variable instruction lengths
An ISA containing only floating-point instructions
A RISC ISA with instructions that are all 4 bytes long
An ISA with only one execution mode and no legacy modes

questions.explanation: x86 is described as a CISC ISA with many complex instructions, variable lengths, and support for legacy modes.

questions.prompt: What is the word size of x86_64, or Intel 64?

options.text: 128 bits
32 bits
16 bits
64 bits

questions.explanation: x86_64, or Intel 64, is the 64-bit extension of the x86 family.

questions.prompt: Which mappings of the x86 extensions are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: Transactional Memory is associated with speculative execution and atomic accesses.
F16C converts half-precision floating-point values.
F16C is the extension for additional stack registers.
VMX supports virtual machines.
VMX performs virtual-to-physical address translation in the MMU.

questions.explanation: VMX, F16C, and Transactional Memory are listed for the purposes stated in a, b, and c, respectively. The other descriptions are not associated with these extensions.

questions.prompt: The 64-bit view of an x86 register is called `RAX`, the 32-bit view `EAX`, the 16-bit view `AX`, and the 8-bit subregisters are called `AH` and `___`.

options.text: AL
EAX
R8
BL

questions.explanation: AH and AL are the two 8-bit subregisters of AX.

questions.prompt: Where does `call` place the return address under the IA-32 calling convention described?

options.text: In the `ra` register
On the stack
In the `eax` register
In a TLB entry

questions.explanation: In the IA-32 call shown, `call` places the return address on the stack. `ra` is the RISC-V convention used for comparison here.

questions.prompt: For this question, consider only the following x86_64 calling convention: the first six parameters are passed, in order, in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, and `r9`; additional parameters are passed on the stack. The return value is in `rax`. Which statements are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The return value is in `rax`.
The first six parameters are in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, and `r9`.
The seventh and every subsequent parameter is passed on the stack.
All parameters must be passed on the stack.
The return value is in `eax`, even in x86_64.

questions.explanation: Under the convention specified in the question, the first six parameters are passed in the listed registers and additional parameters are passed on the stack. The return value is in `rax`.

questions.prompt: With base-relative addressing: effective address = register contents + ___.

options.text: Operand size
Offset
Page number
Return address

questions.explanation: The base-register address is shifted by the offset to obtain the effective address.

questions.prompt: RISC-V supports direct addressing, in which the memory address itself appears in the instruction.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Direct addressing is marked “no” for RISC-V in the table; register-indirect and displacement addressing are supported.

questions.prompt: What does `add edx, eax` do in the x86 two-address form described?

options.text: `eax = edx + eax`
The value in `edx` is written to memory.
`edx = edx + eax`
`edx = eax`

questions.explanation: In this two-address form, the first operand is both the destination and a source; the result overwrites `edx`.

questions.prompt: After which step does Program B resume execution?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["Programm A unterbrechen"] --> S["Zustand sichern"]
  S --> P["Scheduler wählt Programm"]
  P --> L["Zustand von B laden"]
  L --> B["Programm B fortsetzen"]
context.caption: Simplified sequence for time sharing

options.text: Only after Program A has finished
Immediately after Program A is interrupted, without a change of state
After the scheduler has selected Program B and loaded its state
Before Program A's state is saved

questions.explanation: The sequence first saves A's state, then selects B and loads B's state before B resumes.

questions.prompt: What role does the MMU play in the virtual memory system described?

options.text: It determines the instruction order for a compiler.
It stores all return addresses for a process.
It translates virtual addresses into physical addresses.
It selects the next program for the scheduler.

questions.explanation: The MMU performs address translation in hardware during memory accesses; the operating system controls the mapping.

questions.prompt: An instruction uses base-relative addressing `EA = Registerinhalt + Offset`. With register contents `0x1000` and offset `0x18`, what effective address results?

options.text: 0x0FE8

questions.explanation: `0x1000 + 0x18 = 0x1018`. The offset is added to the base.

questions.prompt: With scaled indexing, `EA = Basis + Index × Operandenlänge`. Given base `0x2000`, index `3`, and an operand size of `4` Byte, what effective address results?
questions.explanation: The index contribution is `3 × 4 = 12 = 0xC`; therefore, `EA = 0x2000 + 0xC = 0x200C`.

questions.prompt: An IA-32 stack frame uses `ebp` as its reference point. According to the layout, what is at `[ebp+8]`?

options.text: The return address
Parameter 2
Parameter 1
A local variable

questions.explanation: In the layout shown, parameter 1 is at `[ebp+8]`, parameter 2 is at `[ebp+12]`, and the return address is at `[ebp+4]`.

questions.prompt: A program executes `c += i` and wants to update `c` in memory. Which statements about the ISA examples shown are correct? Select all correct statements.

options.text: With `add edx, eax`, the result is stored in a new third register.
x86 can operate directly on memory with `add DWORD PTR [ebp-0x10], eax`.
RISC-V performs the same memory access directly with a single `add` instruction.
RISC-V typically requires `lw`, `add`, and `sw` for this.

questions.explanation: The x86 example allows addition directly at a memory location. RISC-V uses a load, a register operation, and a store for this; `add edx, eax` also overwrites the first operand.

questions.prompt: A loop starts with `i=0` and `c=0`. In each iteration, it adds `i` to `c`, increments `i` by 1, and continues as long as the new `i ≤ 9`. What is the final value of `c`?
questions.explanation: The loop adds the values from 0 through 9, inclusive. Their sum is 45; checking after the increment causes the loop to stop at `i=10`.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of `add [ebp-0x10], eax` in the x86 code shown?

options.text: The memory contents are copied to `eax`, without addition.
The instruction compares the memory contents with `eax` and sets flags.
The value of `eax` is added to the memory contents at `[ebp-0x10]`; the result remains there.
The value of `eax` is appended to the address `[ebp-0x10]`.

questions.explanation: The instruction shown operates directly on memory: it adds `eax` to the value in memory and overwrites that value there.

questions.prompt: In RISC-V `Vectored` mode, the entry address for asynchronous interrupts is `Einsprungadresse = BASE + 4 × cause`. With `BASE = 0x1000` and `cause = 7`, what entry address results?
questions.explanation: `4 × 7 = 28 = 0x1C`; added to `0x1000`, this gives `0x101C`.

questions.prompt: In X/W/R order, the pattern `101` means read and ___.

options.text: A pointer to the next table level
write only
execute
write

questions.explanation: `101` sets X and R: the page is executable and readable, but not writable.

questions.prompt: A virtual page is mapped to physical page number `0x12345`. With 4-KiB pages, the offset `0xABC` remains unchanged. What physical address results?

options.text: 0x12345ABC
0x12344ABC
0xABC12345

questions.explanation: The physical page base is `0x12345 × 0x1000 = 0x12345000`. Adding the unchanged offset `0xABC` gives `0x12345ABC`.

questions.prompt: In the translation shown, no entry is found in the TLB. Which step follows in the diagram?

context.content:
flowchart TD
  VA["Virtuelle Adresse"] --> T{"Übersetzung im TLB?"}
  T -->|Ja| C{"Eintrag und Zugriff gültig?"}
  T -->|Nein| W["Seitentabellen auslesen"]
  W --> C
  C -->|Ja| PA["Physische Adresse"]
  C -->|Nein| E["Exception"]
  PA --> M["Speicherzugriff"]
context.caption: Schematic sequence for a TLB hit or access fault

options.text: The offset is replaced by the physical page number.
The page tables are read.
The data access happens immediately without translation.
The scheduler selects another process.

questions.explanation: On a TLB miss, the page tables are read; the entry and access are then checked.

questions.prompt: For this question, use the following RISC-V system call convention: for a system call using `ecall`, the system call number is in `a7`, and the parameters are passed in `a0` through `a6`. Where are the number and parameters?

options.text: Number in `a0`, parameters in `a1` through `a7`
Number in `sp`, parameters in `t0` through `t6`
Number on the stack, parameters in `ra`
Number in `a7`, parameters in `a0` through `a6`

questions.explanation: The convention specified in the question places the number in `a7` and the parameters in `a0` through `a6`.

questions.prompt: A single-level Sv32 page table contains `2^20` entries of 4 Byte each. How much memory does it require per process?

options.text: 4 KiB
1 MiB
4 MiB
4 GiB

questions.explanation: `2^20 × 4 Byte = 2^22 Byte`, or 4 MiB.

questions.prompt: In Sv32, `VA = 0x00403ABC` is split into two 10-bit VPN fields and a 12-bit offset. What is the value of `VPN[1]`?

options.text: 0xABC

questions.explanation: The upper 10 bits of the virtual page number give `VPN[1]=1`; the middle VPN field is 3 and the offset is `0xABC`.

questions.prompt: For `VA = 0x00403ABC`, the page tables provide physical page number `0x12345`. With 4-KiB pages, the offset remains unchanged. What physical address results?

options.text: 0x12344ABC
0x00403ABC
0x12345ABC

questions.explanation: The page number gives the physical base `0x12345000`; the virtual offset `0xABC` is preserved. Together, these give `0x12345ABC`.

questions.prompt: The access bits are ordered X, W, R (execute, write, read). A pattern labeled “reserved” is not a valid access permission and must not be interpreted as a combination of its set individual bits. Which statements about the table are correct? Select all correct statements.

context.content:
| X/W/R | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `000` | Pointer to the next table level |
| `001` | Read only |
| `011` | Read and write |
| `100` | Execute only |
| `101` | Read and execute |
| `111` | Read, write, and execute |
| `010` / `110` | Reserved: not a valid access permission |
context.caption: Meaning of the X/W/R patterns

options.text: `100` allows execute only.
`011` allows read and write.
`000` is a pointer to the next table level.
`110` allows read and write.
`010` means write only.

questions.explanation: In X/W/R order, `011` means read and write, `100` means execute only, and `000` is a pointer to the next table level. `010` and `110` are reserved, so they are not valid access permissions.

questions.prompt: A process is running in user mode. For this access, `U=1` allows access in user mode, while `U=0` marks a privileged page. The page-table entry is valid, but `U=0`. What happens when the page is accessed?

options.text: The access is automatically switched to system mode.
The access proceeds if the TLB has a hit.
An exception is raised.
The MMU automatically sets `U` to 1.

questions.explanation: A privileged page cannot be used in user mode. A valid entry or TLB hit does not bypass the access check.

questions.prompt: Sv39 has three page-table levels. Without a TLB, how many page-table accesses are needed for a translation before the actual data access?

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.explanation: Sv39 uses three table levels. Without a TLB, three page-table accesses are therefore needed, in addition to the actual data access.

questions.prompt: A program requests new virtual memory, but no physical page is assigned initially. What happens on the first access?

options.text: The access is permanently rejected because virtual pages cannot receive frames.
An exception causes the operating system to find a frame and add the page-table entry.
The scheduler automatically copies the page into the TLB.
The virtual address is used unchanged as the physical address.

questions.explanation: With lazy allocation, a physical page is assigned only on the first access. The resulting exception prompts the operating system to find a frame and update the table.

questions.prompt: Physical memory is full, and a new page needs to be loaded. Which steps match the paging sequence described? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The operating system selects a page and marks it as absent.
The selected page is written to disk; its frame can be used for the new page.
A later access to the swapped-out page raises an exception so it can be loaded back.
The TLB is used as the disk area for the swapped-out page.
All operating-system pages must be swapped out first.

questions.explanation: With paging, a selected page is swapped out and its frame is reassigned. A later access to the swapped-out page triggers an exception, after which it can be loaded back.

source.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

questions.prompt: A valid Sv32 leaf entry at the first level can point directly to a large 4-MiB page.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: In Sv32, a leaf entry at the first level points directly to a large 4-MiB page instead of to another table.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish interrupts from exceptions? Select all correct statements.

options.text: An exception can never be triggered by an explicit system call.
Interrupts and exceptions are both always synchronous errors caused by an instruction.
An interrupt is asynchronous and can be triggered by an external event.
A timer event is an example of an interrupt.
An exception is synchronous and associated with an executed instruction.

questions.explanation: Interrupts arise asynchronously from external events such as timer or I/O events. Exceptions are synchronous; an explicit system call is given as a possible example.

questions.prompt: Why are page tables and certain areas of the operating system pinned during the paging process described?

options.text: So they are not swapped out.
So the scheduler deletes them at every context switch.
So they automatically receive identical addresses in all virtual address spaces.
So the TLB treats them as executable instructions.

questions.explanation: Pinned pages remain in physical memory. Examples include page tables, parts of the operating system, and pages for devices without an MMU.

source.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

questions.prompt: A program calls a function, which in turn calls another function. In RISC-V, `jal ra, ...` stores the return address in `ra`; in IA-32, `call` places it on the stack. What must the RISC-V code account for when making the nested call?

options.text: Save the current return address in `ra` before the next `jal` overwrites it.
Copy the return address to `eax` because IA-32 uses `ra`.
Save `ra` because `call` places the address on the stack in RISC-V.
Nothing: `jal` places each return address in its own register automatically.

questions.explanation: Another `jal` overwrites `ra`, so any return address that is still needed must be saved beforehand. In IA-32, `call` instead places the return address on the stack.

questions.prompt: A virtual address `0x00403ABC` is mapped to physical page number `0x12345` with a page size of 4 KiB. The offset is preserved during translation. Read four bytes starting at the resulting physical address, in ascending address order. Little-endian means here that the byte at the lowest address forms bits 7–0, the next byte forms bits 15–8, and so on. What 32-bit value do you get?

context.caption: Bytes in memory in ascending address order

questions.explanation: The offset of the virtual address is `0xABC`. The physical address is therefore `0x12345 × 0x1000 + 0xABC = 0x12345ABC`. The bytes at this address and the next three addresses are `78 56 34 12`. In little-endian order, this gives `0x12345678`.

questions.prompt: An array of 4-byte elements starts at virtual address `0x00403000`. Element 2 is at `Basis + Index × Elementgröße`. The virtual page is mapped to physical page number `0x12345`; the offset is preserved. What is the physical address of element 2?
questions.explanation: Element 2 is at `0x00403000 + 2 × 4 = 0x00403008`, so its offset is `0x008`. The physical page base is `0x12345000`; therefore, the physical address is `0x12345008`.

questions.prompt: A timer interrupts Program A so that the operating system can run Program B. Which statements match the time-sharing process described? Select all correct statements.

options.text: The scheduler selects which program runs next.
B's state does not need to be loaded before B resumes.
The operating system saves, among other things, A's registers, SP, and PC.
Program A can switch directly to system mode by executing arbitrary privileged code.
A timer event is an asynchronous interrupt.

questions.explanation: Time sharing saves the state of the interrupted program, lets the scheduler select the next program, and loads its state. A timer is an external, asynchronous interrupt event; user code cannot arbitrarily assume privileged rights.

questions.prompt: A process uses only a small part of its virtual address space with Sv32. Why can multilevel page tables save memory in this case?

options.text: Each process automatically gets larger physical frames.
The TLB permanently takes over the page table.
Unused table areas do not need to be created.
Virtual addresses are shortened to 12 bits.

questions.explanation: Multilevel tables make it possible to create tables only for areas that are actually used. A single-level Sv32 table would require 4 MiB per process.

questions.prompt: An instruction is fetched in user mode from a page. The entry is valid, and `U=1` allows access in user mode. The X/W/R bits are ordered as execute/write/read, so `101` means execute and read. Is access allowed?

options.text: No, `101` allows write and execute only.
Yes, the page is readable and executable in user mode.
Yes, but only if the entry is invalid.
No, `U=1` prohibits instruction accesses.

questions.explanation: In X/W/R order, `101` means execute and read. With a valid entry and `U=1`, the instruction access is allowed in user mode.

questions.prompt: A TLB hit provides a valid translation, but the entry allows reading and prohibits writing. The process attempts a store. What happens?

options.text: The offset is set to zero and the store is retried.
The scheduler automatically sets the write bit.
The store succeeds because the TLB had a hit.
An exception is raised because the write access is not permitted.

questions.explanation: A TLB hit provides the translation but does not bypass access protection. A write to a read-only page raises an exception.

questions.prompt: Two accesses raise an exception: Access A targets a virtual page that has never been assigned physical memory; Access B targets a page that was previously swapped out. Which statements correctly distinguish the cases? Select all correct statements.

options.text: Both exceptions can be part of page management.
For A, lazy allocation can assign a frame for the first time.
For B, the MMU is responsible for reading the page from disk by itself.
For B, the operating system can load the swapped-out page back from disk.
For A, a page must be loaded back from disk.

questions.explanation: Lazy allocation assigns a previously unbacked virtual page on its first access. For an access to a swapped-out page, the operating system must retrieve the page; in both cases, the exception can initiate the management process.

questions.prompt: Access protection can be used deliberately to catch, for example, array overflows as exceptions during debugging.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The notes mention deliberately blocking accesses to detect array overflows and underflows during debugging.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of instruction formats is correct?

options.text: In the three-address form, the destination necessarily overwrites one of the two sources.
x86 is a three-address register-register ISA; RISC-V is a two-address memory ISA.
x86 can use the destination as a source in the two-address form; RISC-V uses a three-address register-register form for `x = y + z`.
Both forms must always store the result directly in memory.

questions.explanation: The x86 register machine described uses the two-address form, in which the destination overlaps with a source. RISC-V uses the Load/Store register-register form, with separate source and destination operands.

questions.prompt: A RISC-V process returns to user mode after an exception. Which statement correctly describes the controlled transition?

options.text: The return can use a privileged instruction such as `mret` or `sret`.
The return happens when the scheduler clears the TLB and loads `ra`.
The transition is impossible because RISC-V has only one mode.
Any user code can obtain arbitrary privileged rights by executing `mret`.

questions.explanation: The transitions between system and user mode described are controlled; `mret` and `sret` are privileged return instructions.

levels.title: Practice: When Addresses Become Part of Everyday Life

questions.prompt: You start an older 32-bit program on an x86_64 PC. Which ISA feature can enable compatibility?

options.text: x86 instructions are always exactly 4 bytes long.
x86 uses only instructions with three operands.
x86_64 retains legacy execution modes.
All x86 registers have the same width.

questions.explanation: x86_64 supplements older word sizes with additional execution modes. Support for a suitable legacy mode can make it possible to run 32-bit programs.

questions.prompt: A database frequently accesses the same memory pages. Which hardware aid can reduce unnecessary page-table accesses?

options.text: The stack pointer points to the program stack.
The scheduler selects the next process.
The swap file stores inactive pages.
The TLB caches recently used address translations.

questions.explanation: The TLB (Translation Look-Aside Buffer) caches recently used translations from virtual to physical addresses. On a hit, the page-table lookup can be skipped.

questions.prompt: A memory page is 4 KiB in size. How many Byte is that? Use 1 KiB = 1024 Byte.
questions.explanation: One KiB is 1024 Byte. Therefore, a 4-KiB page contains 4 × 1024 = 4096 Byte. The page size also determines how many bits are needed for the offset.

questions.prompt: While you type on your smartphone, other programs keep running. Which two events are examples of interrupts arriving from outside?

options.text: A hardware timer signals.
The program's memory access violates a permission.
The running program executes an invalid instruction.
A network packet arrives.

questions.explanation: Interrupts arise asynchronously from external events such as network or timer signals. An invalid instruction and an unauthorized memory access are associated with an executed instruction and raise exceptions.

questions.prompt: You reserve a large virtual memory area for a simulation but initially use only a small part of it. How can the operating system avoid providing a physical frame for every page immediately?

options.text: It uses lazy allocation and assigns a frame only on the first access.
It stores every virtual address in the TLB permanently.
It disables the MMU for the program.
It immediately swaps all pages to disk.

questions.explanation: With lazy allocation, a virtual page receives a physical frame only after its first access. An access to a page that has not yet been provided can raise an exception, which the operating system handles.

questions.prompt: A page is 4 KiB in size. How many address bits are needed for the offset within the page? Use 1 KiB = 1024 Byte.
questions.explanation: 4 KiB is 4 × 1024 = 4096 = 2¹² Byte. Therefore, 12 offset bits are needed; these bits remain unchanged when translating a virtual address to a physical address.

questions.prompt: Physical memory is full. The operating system marks a long-unused page as absent and writes it to a storage device. Later, the program accesses it again. Which concept does this illustrate?

options.text: Register renaming: a register receives a new name.
Paging: the page is loaded back when needed.
Time sharing: the scheduler switches processes.
Lazy allocation: the page receives memory for the first time.

questions.explanation: With paging, a selected page can be swapped out and marked as absent. A later access raises an exception so the operating system can load the page back.

source.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

questions.prompt: A hypothetical method translates a virtual address through three page-table levels without a TLB hit. A data value is then read from memory. How many memory accesses are needed in total? Count one access per table level and one for the data value.
questions.explanation: The three table levels require three memory accesses. The subsequent read of the data value brings the total to four accesses.

questions.prompt: A smartphone app runs without privileged rights and wants to read a file. How does it request an operating-system service in a controlled way?

options.text: By bypassing the TLB and changing the page table itself.
By permanently switching the processor to system mode.
Through a system call that the operating system can check.
By executing privileged device instructions directly in user mode.

questions.explanation: A system call enables a controlled transition from user mode to the operating system. The operating system can check parameters and permissions before providing the service.

questions.prompt: You are reading x86 assembly. Before the instruction, `eax` contains 7 and `ebx` contains 5. What is true after `add eax, ebx`?

options.text: eax contains 12 afterward.
ebx contains 12 afterward.
eax remains 7; the result is in a new register.
The instruction writes 12 directly to memory.

questions.explanation: In this x86 two-address form, the destination is also a source: the instruction adds `ebx` to `eax` and overwrites `eax` with 12. In a three-address register form, the sources and destination would be separate.
